references.text: Describes how the "sons of God" saw that human daughters were beautiful and took wives from among them – the direct context leading up to verse 4.
Follows the events in verse 4 and describes God's judgment on human wickedness on earth.
Nimrod is described as the first "gibbor" (mighty man/heroe) on earth, with a direct linguistic connection to "gibborim" in Gen 6:4.
The Nephilim are mentioned again as the great giants that the spies saw in the land of Canaan – the only other occurrence of the word "nephilim" in the OT.
Refers to the Emim as a large and numerous people group, counted among the Rephaim – part of the broader giant tradition in the OT.
Refers to King Og of Bashan as the last of the Rephaim, a group of giants within the broader tradition linked to the Nephilim.
Peter writes about angels who sinned and were cast down into chains of darkness – a central reference to the tradition of fallen angels that may be connected to the "sons of God" in Gen 6.
Christ proclaimed to spirits in prison who were disobedient in Noah's days – a connection to the disobedient spiritual beings from before the flood.
Jude mentions angels who did not keep their proper domain but abandoned their rightful dwelling, which is traditionally linked to the "sons of God" in Gen 6:1-4.
